newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook- Crashing prices prompt cuts.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook- Crashing prices prompt cuts.

text.p: Plunging prices and a bearish outlook for oil products in Asia, particularly gas oil, has prompted refiners to cut production in Singapore, industry sources said on Monday.

"Refiners are now experiencing very negative margins of around $1 for Arab Light (crude)," said a trader with a European major. "Although margins only turned bad very recently, there is talk about cutting runs as the outlook does not look too bright."
Shell Singapore said on Friday it had indefinitely cut runs at its 435,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery by 4,000 tonnes per day (30,000-bpd).
Esso Singapore on Monday said it cut runs over the weekend at its 230,000-bpd refinery by 20 to 25 percent.

Traders said weaker products prices across the barrel were responsible. Gas oil values crashed nearly $4.00 per barrel last week and paper flipped into contango, pressured by as much as one million barrels on offer.
"The (gas oil) market is flooded," one broker said. "There is talk of two gas oil cargoes floating off Singapore and one off China which can not find a home."
But traders said prices showed some signs of steadying on Friday. Gas oil found bids -- although nothing traded -- and fuel oil found support from the refinery cut news and some China enquiries.
But this week might rely on how well the market absorbs the surplus cargoes on offer.

Diesel sellers were looking to India, whose March diesel buying tender closes on Wednesday. India took a hefty 855,000 tonnes for February deliveries after holding back purchases for several months late last year.
And while Singapore refiners have placed unsold supplies with independent storage terminals, ullage was tight in both China and Hong Kong, traders said.
Chinese requirements have been covered for the Chinese New Year in early February and regional demand is otherwise muted.

Singapore fuel oil, which plunged by $10 per tonne last week, amid aggressive selling of regular supplies from Iran, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela. Ample South Korean supplies sought outlets in the bunker market but with limited success.
Naphtha prices also edged down in a correction from new six-year highs of $252 per tonne on Tokyo's open-spec forward contract and $26.30 in Singapore on January 9.
But naphtha fell faster than crude, reflecting selling of the wide naphtha crack for first-half March open-spec naphtha with March Brent crude, which had widened to as much as $70 a tonne.
By the end of the week it had narrowed to around $64, when normally it trades $50 to $55, traders said.
Traders said they expected the correction to continue this week, bringing the crack in to the high $50s, or low $60s.
The high spot naphtha price also prompted buyers to source supplies from term cargoes, leaving at least four spot cargoes available in February.
Meanwhile, naphtha demand was stable even though some Japanese petrochemical companies said they have cut production by 10 percent.
"Ten percent is a huge cut, but there's no big concrete evidence. They are still buying," said a western trader.

Indonesia was expected to allocate an additional 200,000 barrels of low sulphur waxy residue (LSWR) in January to its initial allocation of 3.5 million barrels. But February supplies were expected to drop amid the shutdown of the 125,000 barrel-per-day Dumai refinery.
